title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
official_title: To amend the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 to include certain retired law enforcement officers in the public safety officers' death benefits program.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) with Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) — a cross-aisle sponsor pairing on public-safety benefits. The measure passed the Senate by Unanimous Consent on July 29, 2025 and was received in the House on August 1, 2025 per the latest recorded action. The 2012 retroactivity window and the fiscal cost of new claims are the most likely points of pushback.
summary: The Public Safety Officers' Benefits program, run by the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Assistance, pays a $250,000 line-of-duty death benefit (adjusted each year for inflation) and matching disability benefit to the families of police, firefighters, and other public safety officers killed or permanently disabled on the job. This bill extends the same benefit to retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled as a direct and proximate result of a targeted attack because of their prior service as an officer.
brief: Adds retired law enforcement officers targeted for their prior service to the federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits program, with claims applying retroactively to attacks on or after January 1, 2012.

top_lines.headline: What the Program Pays
subs: $250,000 death benefit, adjusted each October for inflation
Same amount payable for permanent and total disability
Interim benefit up to $6,000 while a claim is pending

top_lines.headline: New Eligibility for Retired Officers
subs: Covers officers who separated in good standing as a law enforcement officer

Attack must be because of the officer's prior law enforcement service

top_lines.headline: Retroactive Window

sections.label: Section 2 — Inclusion of Certain Retired Public Safety Officers in the Public Safety Officers' Death Benefits Program

items.main: Adds a new subsection (p) to 34 U.S.C. 10281 making retired law enforcement officers eligible for the Public Safety Officers' Benefits program when they die or become permanently and totally disabled from a targeted attack tied to their prior service.
items.detail: A "retired law enforcement officer" is defined as an individual who separated in good standing as a law enforcement officer in an official capacity at a public agency, with or without compensation. Eligibility requires that the death or permanent-and-total disability be the direct and proximate result of a personal injury from a targeted attack because of the officer's service as a law enforcement officer. Claims are processed by the Bureau of Justice Assistance under the existing benefits framework.

items.main: Sets a retroactive effective date so the new eligibility reaches back to targeted attacks occurring on or after January 1, 2012.
items.detail: The amendments take effect on the date of enactment and apply to any matter pending before the Bureau of Justice Assistance on that date, or filed or accruing after it. As an exception to that general rule, the amendment applies to any action taken against a retired law enforcement officer on or after January 1, 2012.

underreported.summary: The bill reaches back nearly 14 years before enactment, applying the new eligibility to any qualifying targeted attack on or after January 1, 2012.
underreported.why_unreported: The section heading names an "exception" to the general effective-date rule, but the operative effect is a broad retroactivity window that opens years of prior incidents to new claim filings — a scope not stated in the bill's short title or Section 2 heading.

gaps: The bill extends eligibility to retired officers but does not define "targeted attack" or list the evidence required to establish that an attack was "because of" the retiree's prior service.

The bill applies retroactively to January 1, 2012 but does not set a filing deadline for pre-enactment claims or address how the Bureau of Justice Assistance should prioritize backlogged retroactive claims against current-year filings.
The bill relies on the existing inflation-adjusted death benefit and disability-benefit mechanism in 34 U.S.C. 10281 but does not authorize additional appropriations to cover the new class of claims.

The bill uses "retired law enforcement officer" only and does not address whether retired firefighters, emergency medical responders, or other public safety officers targeted for prior service qualify.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Booker
featured_quotes.text: So, Mr. President, this casts a shadow over everything that was just said because I support these bills. Why do I support these bills? Because the officers of the State of New Jersey are going to benefit from them because Donald Trump hasn't targeted these and cut these, and these are things that are going to help all officers. That is what this body should do--not pick and choose one State over another, not pit one State against another, not pit so-called blue States over so-called red States. It is the United States of America.

added: New subsection 34 U.S.C. 10281(p) — eligibility for retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled from a targeted attack tied to their prior service
modified: 34 U.S.C. 10281 (Public Safety Officers' Death Benefits — Payment of death benefits) — expanded to cover certain retired officers, with retroactive reach to targeted attacks on or after January 1, 2012
